title: Networking theory
description: Reason about layers, transport, addressing, and the path of a request.

modules.title: A request from browser to server
modules.description: Reason about layers, transport, addressing, and the path of a request.

lessons.title: Follow the layers
lessons.body:
### Different layers answer different questions
HTTP describes an application request. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream between endpoints. IP supplies addressing and routing across networks. A link layer moves frames over a local connection.

### Keep names separate from addresses
DNS resolves a hostname to records such as IP addresses. A destination port identifies the service endpoint. These steps do different jobs.

### A useful debugging habit
Ask whether name resolution, connectivity, transport setup, TLS, or the application request failed instead of calling every failure a server error.

lessons.title: TCP, reliability & TLS
lessons.body:
### TCP provides a byte stream
TCP uses sequence numbers and acknowledgments to track data, and retransmits when necessary. Applications still need message framing because one application write does not correspond to one read.

### TLS has a separate job
TLS protects the connection and authenticates the peer according to its configured trust model. It does not replace HTTP semantics.

### Know which stack you are tracing
An HTTPS request over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 usually uses TCP plus TLS. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, so its connection setup differs.

exercises.title: Trace an HTTPS request
exercises.prompt: Trace a fresh HTTPS request using HTTP/1.1 over TCP, with no cached DNS result and no reusable connection. Explain the role of DNS, the TCP handshake, TLS, and HTTP. Then describe what a reused connection avoids.
hints: DNS is about finding an address.
TCP and TLS have separate setup and guarantees.
Avoid assuming all HTTPS uses TCP.
exercises.answer: Resolve the hostname, choose an address, establish TCP, perform the TLS handshake and certificate verification, send the HTTP request, and receive the response. A reusable connection can avoid another TCP and TLS setup; DNS caching can also avoid another lookup. Routing and link-layer forwarding carry traffic throughout. HTTP/3 has a different transport sequence.
